answers.explanation: Spreading makes the signal harder to jam, harder to eavesdrop on, and better at surviving noise.
Layer 1, the physical layer: it changes how bits become radio waves.
Early Wi-Fi turned each bit into 11 chips with the Barker code. Hopping between frequencies is FHSS.
The remaining chips still match one pattern far better than the other.
Without the sequence, a listener hears fragments, and a jammer only hits the hops that land on its frequency.
Only about 1 hop in 79 lands on the jammed channel.
Many users share the band at once, each picked out by its code, as in the room-of-languages analogy from chapter 3.
Senders get time slots, and the slots can be on different carriers. Satellite networks use it.
A film star and a composer, to keep radio-guided torpedoes from being jammed.
